flagged.evidence: The Statement says only `Let 0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots be measurable and suppose f_n\uparrow f almost everywhere. Then \int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.` This does not require `f` itself to be measurable. On the non-complete space `([0,1], \mathcal B([0,1]), \lambda|_{\mathcal B})`, let `C` be the Cantor set, choose a non-Borel `A\subseteq C`, set `f_n:=0` for all `n`, and set `f:=\chi_A`. Then `f_n\uparrow f` almost everywhere because `f=0` on `[0,1]\setminus C` and `C` is null, but `f` is not measurable, so `\int f\,d\mu` in the Statement is not defined. The proof also uses `g:=f\chi_{X\setminus N}` and `f\chi_N` in step 2.1, which are not licensed without measurability of `f`.

Hypothesis 4 states only `|\partial_t f(x,t)|\le g(x)` `for every t\in I and almost every x`. But step 2.1 argues: `For almost every x and every n ... The derivative bound in the hypotheses gives |q_n(x)|\le g(x). Therefore [L1] applies to (q_n).` The mean-value point used for `q_n(x)` lies at an intermediate parameter depending on `x` and `n`, so this domination requires one null set on which the derivative bound holds for every relevant `t`. The stated quantifier order allows the exceptional null set to depend on `t`, which does not license the uniform a.e. bound on the whole sequence `(q_n)` needed to invoke dominated convergence.

Step 1.1 defines `I_k := (2^{-k-1},2^{-k}]`, but step 2.1 then identifies `\bigcup_{k<n} I_k = [2^{-n},1]`. That set equality is false: the point `2^{-n}` belongs to `[2^{-n},1]` but to no `I_k` with `k<n`, so the union is `(2^{-n},1]`, not `[2^{-n},1]`.
